title: A sound can seem to rise forever without getting any higher
body: A Shepard tone stacks the same note in several octaves and slides them all upward together. As the highest copy climbs it fades out, while a new copy fades in at the bottom, so your ear always has a middle to follow and **never hears a top or a bottom**: the pitch seems to climb endlessly yet ends where it started, a musical barber’s pole. Roger Shepard described the illusion in 1964, Jean-Claude Risset made a smoothly gliding version, and the score of Christopher Nolan’s Dunkirk uses it to create a sense of intensity that never stops building.

slides.alt: A chart of pitch against time showing six parallel rising diagonal lines, staggered in time. Each line is faint at the bottom, bright in the middle and faint again at the top, so as one copy fades out at the top another is already rising.
slides.caption: Octave copies fade in low and out high, so the climb never ends.

slides.heading: How your ear is fooled
slides.text: Each octave copy fades in at the bottom of the range and fades out at the top, so you never hear a scale start or finish. Your brain tracks the strong middle tones and hears one endless climb, like watching the stripes on a barber’s pole.

steps.label: Stack the same note in several octaves
The top copy fades out as it climbs
A new copy fades in at the bottom

slides.prompt: A 1996 video game used this illusion, a Shepard scale, to make a staircase feel endless. Which one?
slides.answer: Super Mario 64: the never-ending stairs in Peach’s Castle
slides.detail: The looping music matches the looping stairs, which go on for ever until the player has collected 70 stars.

slides.heading: Oldest first
slides.explanation: Shepard’s paper came out in 1964; Risset’s continuous glissando followed; Super Mario 64 arrived in 1996 and Dunkirk in 2017.
